desc:
Given a binary search tree and an integer target, return the value stored in the tree that is closest to target, that is, the value x with the smallest |x - target|.

If two values are equally close, return the smaller one. The target itself does not have to be in the tree.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [5,2,7,-1,3,6] is the tree whose root 5 has left child 2 and right child 7; node 2 has no left child and right child 3; node 7 has left child 6 and no right child.

Example 1

tree = [10,5,15,2,7,12,20], target = 13
Output: 12
12 is at distance 1, 15 is at distance 2.

Example 2

tree = [8,4,12,2,6,10,14], target = 9
Output: 8
8 and 10 are both at distance 1, so the smaller one wins.
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000, all values distinct; the tree is a valid BST
hints: Scanning all the nodes and keeping the best one is O(n). The BST ordering lets you do better on a balanced tree.
Search for the target as if you wanted to insert it. Every node on that search path is a candidate for the closest value.
Walk down from the root: update the best candidate (smaller distance, or equal distance and smaller value) at every node, then go left if target < node, otherwise right.
editorial: The closest value is either the largest value not above the target (its floor) or the smallest value not below it (its ceiling). Both of them lie on the search path of the target, because the path passes every node where the answer could still change sides. So walk down once, compare each visited value with the best so far, and move left when the target is smaller than the node and right otherwise.
For ties, compare the pair (distance, value) so that the smaller value wins at equal distance. The walk costs O(h) time and O(1) memory beyond the parsed tree.
